Claim: Adoption could join heirship/property arrangements to lifetime support.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Clauses establish obligations, not their performance.
Generalization limit: Two contractual examples, not frequency or exclusive motive.
Project relevance: Continuity involved obligations as well as titles.

Claim: A woman explicitly designated nadītu acted as adopter and disposed of assets attributed to her father’s gift.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Adopter’s status is explicit; Narubtum’s purported religious status is not.
Generalization limit: One named adopter; no general rule for all women or nadītu.
Project relevance: Female agency in intergenerational transmission.

Claim: Adoptive affiliation did not require erasure of earlier identifying parentage in surviving records.
Period/date: Lipit-Enlil d; Rīm-Sîn 43 to Samsu-iluna 4; undated OB
Primary evidence: D01 obv. 3–6; D12 obv. 2; D14 seal; D18 seal
Counterevidence/disagreement: Filiation is an identification convention, not proof of ongoing residence or support.
Generalization limit: Recorded names, not a complete map of social ties.
Project relevance: Multiple relationship histories remained legible.

Claim: Adoption/heir appointment could occur alongside marriage and involve several named heirs.
Secondary interpretation: S01 reconsiders payment and family reconstruction
Counterevidence/disagreement: Damaged payment clause; four heirs’ common maternity not established.
Generalization limit: One combined agreement; no general stepchild adoption rule.
Project relevance: Conjugal and succession arrangements could intersect.

Claim: Likely identification of Ninurta-muballiṭ links heir appointment in year 6 to a further adoption in year 11.
Counterevidence/disagreement: No explicit cancellation or concurrent validity of earlier affiliation.
Generalization limit: Identity linkage stronger than reconstruction of legal coexistence.
Project relevance: Affiliations could be renegotiated over a life course.

Claim: The revised date of Mannum’s partition is year 10 rather than year 23.
Primary evidence: D06; S01 pp. 26–27 re-edition; D07 contextual cross-check
Counterevidence/disagreement: Older digital date reading persists; no new photographic collation made here.
Generalization limit: Edition-based chronology of this tablet.
Project relevance: Changes the order of inheritance and subsequent acquisitions.

Claim: An adoption-only account of Mannum’s resources is not established by the consulted sequence.
Secondary interpretation: S01 rejects inheritance being too late to matter
Counterevidence/disagreement: Chronological possibility does not prove how particular purchases were financed.
Generalization limit: No quantified causal wealth model or complete accounts.
Project relevance: Multiple transmission channels must remain analytically distinct.

Claim: A mixed estate could be partitioned through itemized allocations and compensation.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Comparable house areas do not make every asset equal or demonstrate universal shares.
Generalization limit: These recorded divisions only.
Project relevance: Fission was selective reallocation, not necessarily total social separation.

Claim: A prior gift to a daughter could require a later settlement with other family claimants.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Not automatically a death-triggered inheritance or standard dowry.
Generalization limit: One documented settlement.
Project relevance: Earlier acts continued to structure later claims.

Claim: Estate division dates cannot automatically be treated as dates of death.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Death is inferred from heirs and sequence, not directly dated.
Generalization limit: Depends on prosopographic identification.
Project relevance: Succession could be temporally extended.

Claim: Inherited built property could be exchanged for fractions of recurring institutional rights.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Service performance, income and residence unrecorded; seal patronym issue.
Generalization limit: One recorded exchange; not a uniform prebend economy.
Project relevance: The composition of transmitted resources could change.

Claim: A retrospective expense settlement transferred an institutional entitlement from heirs to the provider.
Primary evidence: D08 expense tablet, examination and transfer
Counterevidence/disagreement: Recognition of expenditure is not a complete account of care or proof of adoptive relation.
Generalization limit: Specific settlement, not a universal filial entitlement.
Project relevance: Claims arising during life could affect a later estate.

Claim: Property could return to an earlier owner’s family through a later conveyance by successor-side parties.
Primary evidence: D11; proposed purchase parallel D10 catalogue-only
Counterevidence/disagreement: Exact identity with D10’s built plot not fully verified.
Generalization limit: Legal chain clearer than exact physical parcel history.
Project relevance: Continuity and recombination could cross family boundaries.

Claim: A mother’s appearance among joint vendors does not by itself establish guardianship or her ownership share.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Text does not fully specify why each vendor had to consent.
Generalization limit: An evidentiary limit, not denial of women’s rights.
Project relevance: Avoids inferring authority or household composition from signatures alone.

Claim: An earlier adoption was invoked in a later division of Narāmtum’s estate.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Retrospective title clause need not be a new adoption between the partitioners.
Generalization limit: Two separated documentary endpoints; intermediate story incompletely verified.
Project relevance: Legal relationships could remain consequential decades later.

Claim: The later estate division included separately named enslaved women and men, with land used as a balancing allocation.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Not evidence that all lived together or that adopted enslaved heirs occur in this sample.
Generalization limit: Recorded allocations; lived experiences and family consequences largely absent.
Project relevance: Transmission affected dependent persons, not only things.

Claim: Perpetual co-ownership, survivorship and continued co-residence are not demonstrated by the partition text alone.
Secondary interpretation: S03 proposes a stronger continuity interpretation
Counterevidence/disagreement: Stronger reconstruction may be testable with the full archive; not disproved universally.
Generalization limit: Conclusion about evidentiary sufficiency, not all actual outcomes.
Project relevance: Separates legal settlement from a continuous residential household.

Claim: Repudiation clauses anticipated termination; one separate court record documents an actual termination process.
Secondary interpretation: S07 revised reading incorporated in D18
Counterevidence/disagreement: Court narrative damaged; no outcome rate or generic fixed penalty established.
Generalization limit: Different documentary stages, not equivalent event counts.
Project relevance: Continuity was legally contestable, not automatic or irreversible.

Claim: The court record extends its exclusion of claims to the rejected heir’s heirs.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Long-term compliance and subsequent litigation not documented.
Generalization limit: The scope of the recorded instrument only.
Project relevance: A rupture could be framed to affect future generations.

Claim: No securely mapped residential continuity is established for the two principal dossiers in this return.
Nippur context: Nippur attribution, often no exact findspot
Primary evidence: D01–D16 provenance fields; D18 has excavation number only
Counterevidence/disagreement: A research access/provenance limitation, not a claim that houses cannot be identified.
Generalization limit: Conclusion limited to sources actually consulted.
Project relevance: Prevents converting legal/prosopographic continuity into co-residence.

Claim: This selected legal corpus cannot supply citywide adoption frequencies or demographic norms.
Period/date: Old Babylonian Nippur; narrow actual coverage
Primary evidence: Document inventory and deduplication; missing observation base
Counterevidence/disagreement: Poor and non-document-producing persons are not adequately represented.
Generalization limit: No representative sampling frame or full corpus enumeration.
Project relevance: Limits prevalence, age, household-size and success-rate claims.

Claim: Continuity is best evidenced here as successive claims and reallocations, not proof of an unchanged resident group.
Period/date: Across the two dossiers and supporting court case
Secondary interpretation: S01/S02 versus stronger reconstruction S03; synthesis here
Counterevidence/disagreement: Residence and daily cooperation may have persisted but are not independently established.
Generalization limit: Analytical synthesis, not a canonical definition of household.
Project relevance: Answers the task without making a simulation design decision.

Claim: A supplementary Nippur-attributed adoption instrument separates heirship transfer from reserved lifetime benefit.
Counterevidence/disagreement: Uncertain local provenance; instrument does not document subsequent actual enjoyment.
Generalization limit: Contractual differentiation in one text, not verified practical control.
Project relevance: Shows why entitlement, timing and benefit cannot simply be equated.

Claim: Repudiation amounts were not identical across the inspected instruments.
Nippur context: Securely attributed D09 versus uncertain-provenance TIM texts
Primary evidence: D09 rev. 3, 11: half mina; D26 rev. 1, 7 and D27 obv. 9, 15: one-third mina
Counterevidence/disagreement: Differences in date, provenance and transaction circumstances preclude a single citywide penalty.
Generalization limit: Numerical contrast only; not a statement of universally enforceable law.
Project relevance: Prevents flattening distinct agreements into one rule.
